CALIFORNIA HOMESTEAD EXEMPTION — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Alex Lee · 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield

PURPOSE OF THIS HOMESTEAD EXEMPTION INFORMATION SHEET
This Information Sheet describes California's automatic homestead exemption for a judgment debtor's principal residence, codified at California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710-704.850 (Enforcement of Judgments, Division 2, Chapter 4, Article 4, “Homestead Exemption”). It covers the statutory definitions of “dwelling” and “homestead,” how the exempt dollar amount is calculated, how this automatic exemption differs from California's separate “declared homestead” recording procedure under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.910-704.995 (Article 5), the court-supervised procedure a judgment creditor must use to force a sale of a homestead dwelling, and how sale proceeds are distributed. It concerns the dwelling located at 123 Main St, Apt 4, Springfield, San Diego County, California, and is prepared by Jordan Alex Lee. This Information Sheet is a general reference describing California statutes; it is not a court filing, a recorded instrument, a claim of exemption, an application for a homestead declaration, or legal advice about whether the exemption, any specific dollar amount, or any specific outcome applies to Jordan Alex Lee's dwelling or circumstances.

STATUTORY DEFINITIONS OF "DWELLING" AND "HOMESTEAD"
California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.710 defines the terms used throughout the homestead exemption statutes. Under § 704.710(a), a “dwelling” means a place where a person resides, and the statute lists examples including a house with its outbuildings and land, a mobilehome, a boat or other waterborne vessel, a condominium, a planned development, a stock cooperative, and a community apartment project. Under § 704.710(c), a “homestead” means the principal dwelling in which the judgment debtor or the judgment debtor's spouse resided on the date the judgment creditor's lien attached to the dwelling, and in which the judgment debtor or spouse resided continuously after that date until a court determines that the dwelling is a homestead. Only a person's principal dwelling can qualify as a homestead under this definition — the statute does not extend the exemption to a second home or investment property that is not the person's principal residence.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "“Dwelling” means a place where a person resides and may include but is not limited to the following:(1) A house together with the outbuildings and the land upon which they are situated.(2) A mobilehome together with the outbuildings and the land upon which they are situated.(3) A boat or other waterborne vessel.(4) A condominium, as defined in Section 783 of the Civil Code.(5) A planned development, as defined in Section 11003 of the Business and Professions Code.(6) A stock cooperative, as defined in Section 11003.2 of the Business and Professions Code.(7) A community apartment project, as defined in Section 11004 of the Business and Professions Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.710(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, definition of “dwelling” for the homestead exemption article (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.710.)
  "“Homestead” means the principal dwelling (1) in which the judgment debtor or the judgment debtor’s spouse resided on the date the judgment creditor’s lien attached to the dwelling, and (2) in which the judgment debtor or the judgment debtor’s spouse resided continuously thereafter until the date of the court determination that the dwelling is a homestead."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.710(c), California Code of Civil Procedure, definition of “homestead” for the homestead exemption article (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.710.)
  Known gap: California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710(a) and 704.710(c) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. Section 704.710 also defines “family unit” (§ 704.710(b)) and “spouse” (§ 704.710(d)) for purposes of this article; those definitions are not described in this Information Sheet. This document states California's statutory definitions; it does not determine whether any specific property is a person's principal dwelling or otherwise qualifies as a homestead.

THE AMOUNT OF THE HOMESTEAD EXEMPTION
California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.730(a) sets the amount of the homestead exemption as the greater of two figures: (1) the countywide median sale price for a single-family home in the calendar year before the year the judgment debtor claims the exemption, capped at $600,000; or (2) $300,000 flat. Section 704.730(b) provides that both the $600,000 cap and the $300,000 floor adjust annually for inflation, beginning January 1, 2022, based on the change in the California Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers published by the Department of Industrial Relations, with each adjusted figure rounded to the nearest $25. This formula — a floor tied to a flat dollar amount and a ceiling tied to countywide median home prices — replaced the flat, status-based dollar amounts (previously keyed to marital status, head-of-household status, or age or disability) that applied under this section before it was amended effective January 1, 2021.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) The amount of the homestead exemption is the greater of the following:(1) The countywide median sale price for a single-family home in the calendar year prior to the calendar year in which the judgment debtor claims the exemption, not to exceed six hundred thousand dollars ($600,000).(2) Three hundred thousand dollars ($300,000)."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.730(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, formula for the homestead exemption amount (floor and ceiling) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.730.)
  "The amounts specified in this section shall adjust annually for inflation, beginning on January 1, 2022, based on the change in the annual California Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers, published by the Department of Industrial Relations, for the most recent one-year period ending on December 31 preceding the adjustment, with each adjusted amount rounded to the nearest twenty-five dollars ($25)."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.730(b), California Code of Civil Procedure, annual inflation adjustment of the homestead exemption amounts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.730.)
  Known gap: California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.730(a) and 704.730(b) are both subsections of the same statutory section and are not independent of one another as sources. The $300,000 and $600,000 figures quoted here are the statutory floor and ceiling as codified in the text fetched for this Information Sheet (the section was last amended by Stats. 2024, Ch. 80, Sec. 24 (SB 1525), effective January 1, 2025); § 704.730(b)'s annual inflation adjustment means the dollar figures a court actually applies as of any given date may be higher than $300,000/$600,000, and those adjusted figures are published administratively rather than restated in the statutory text itself. This Information Sheet states only the statutory floor, ceiling, and adjustment mechanism — it does not state a current-year adjusted dollar figure. Determining the countywide median sale price for a particular county and year, and therefore the precise exemption amount that would apply to any specific dwelling, requires consulting county-specific data not addressed here.

THIS AUTOMATIC EXEMPTION IS DISTINCT FROM A RECORDED "DECLARED HOMESTEAD"
The homestead exemption described in this Information Sheet, under California Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.710-704.850 (Article 4), applies without any recorded declaration: Code of Civil Procedure § 704.720(a) states that a homestead is exempt from a forced sale to the extent provided elsewhere in that article, and § 704.740(a) requires a judgment creditor seeking to sell a debtor's dwelling to obtain a court order for sale, with the dwelling exemption “determined under this article” — that is, in the court proceeding itself, at the time enforcement is sought, rather than through any prior recorded filing. California law separately provides an optional “declared homestead” procedure under Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.910-704.995 (Article 5). Under § 704.920, a dwelling becomes a “declared homestead” only by recording a homestead declaration with the county recorder of the county where the dwelling is located, and only “from and after the time of recording.” The declared homestead is a separate statutory mechanism, defined and governed by its own set of Article 5 sections, and this Information Sheet does not describe what additional or different protections a declared homestead provides.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "A homestead is exempt from sale under this division to the extent provided in Section 704.800."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.720(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, existence of the homestead exemption from forced sale (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.720.)
  "Except as provided in subdivision (b), the interest of a natural person in a dwelling may not be sold under this division to enforce a money judgment except pursuant to a court order for sale obtained under this article and the dwelling exemption shall be determined under this article."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.740(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, requirement of a court order for sale and article-based exemption determination (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.740.)
  "A dwelling in which an owner or spouse of an owner resides may be selected as a declared homestead pursuant to this article by recording a homestead declaration in the office of the county recorder of the county where the dwelling is located. From and after the time of recording, the dwelling is a declared homestead for the purposes of this article."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.920, California Code of Civil Procedure, recording requirement to create a declared homestead (Article 5) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.920.)
  Known gap: Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.720 and 704.740 (Article 4) and § 704.920 (Article 5) are separately numbered, independently enacted sections in different articles of the Enforcement of Judgments Law, not subsections of one section, so they are independent sources. Neither § 704.720(a) nor § 704.740(a) contains the words “automatic” or “no recording required”; the statement that the Article 4 exemption requires no recorded declaration is drawn from the structure of Article 4 itself — it conditions the exemption on a court determination made in an enforcement proceeding, not on any recorded document — contrasted with Article 5's express recording requirement in § 704.920. This Information Sheet does not describe the declared homestead's specific requirements, effects, or any protections it provides beyond what Article 4 already provides; a reader whose questions concern a declared homestead specifically should look to §§ 704.910-704.995 directly, which are outside this document's scope.

HOW A FORCED SALE OF A HOMESTEAD DWELLING WORKS
Before a judgment creditor can force the sale of a debtor's homestead dwelling, California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.750(a) requires the levying officer, promptly after levying on the dwelling, to notify the judgment creditor that the property will be released unless the creditor acts; the judgment creditor then has 20 days after that notice to apply to the court for an order for sale of the dwelling and to file a copy of the application with the levying officer, or the levying officer must release the dwelling. If a sale does go forward under a resulting court order, § 704.800(a) provides that if no bid at the sale exceeds the amount of the homestead exemption plus any additional amount necessary to satisfy all liens and encumbrances on the property — including but not limited to any attachment or judgment lien — the homestead is not sold; it is released, and the same judgment creditor cannot bring a new application for a court order for sale of that homestead for a period of one year.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Promptly after a dwelling is levied upon (other than a dwelling described in subdivision (b) of Section 704.740), the levying officer shall serve notice on the judgment creditor that the levy has been made and that the property will be released unless the judgment creditor complies with the requirements of this section. Service shall be made personally or by mail. Within 20 days after service of the notice, the judgment creditor shall apply to the court for an order for sale of the dwelling and shall file a copy of the application with the levying officer. If the judgment creditor does not file the copy of the application for an order for sale of the dwelling within the allowed time, the levying officer shall release the dwelling."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.750(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, notice after levy and the judgment creditor's 20-day deadline to apply for a court order for sale (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.750.)
  "If no bid is received at a sale of a homestead pursuant to a court order for sale that exceeds the amount of the homestead exemption plus any additional amount necessary to satisfy all liens and encumbrances on the property, including but not limited to any attachment or judgment lien, the homestead shall not be sold and shall be released and is not thereafter subject to a court order for sale upon subsequent application by the same judgment creditor for a period of one year."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.800(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, minimum-bid rule requiring a bid to exceed the exemption plus liens and encumbrances (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.800.)
  Known gap: Code of Civil Procedure §§ 704.750 and 704.800 are separately numbered, independently enacted sections and are independent sources. Section 704.800(a)'s own text names “liens and encumbrances on the property” broadly and gives “attachment or judgment lien” only as non-exclusive examples; in the text fetched, it does not separately itemize a mortgage or deed of trust, a mechanic's lien, or a property tax lien by name. A consensual lien such as a mortgage or deed of trust recorded against the dwelling is commonly understood to be an “encumbrance on the property” within this provision's plain language, but this Information Sheet has not independently verified statutory carve-outs specific to mechanic's liens or property tax liens against a primary source, and does not state whether those particular lien types are treated any differently — that determination is outside what §§ 704.750 and 704.800 were verified to say. This Information Sheet also does not describe the court hearing procedure by which the exemption amount is determined and the order for sale is granted or denied, only the notice/application timeline and the minimum-bid rule described above.

DISTRIBUTION OF SALE PROCEEDS WHEN A HOMESTEAD IS SOLD
California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.850(a) sets out the order in which a levying officer must distribute the proceeds of a homestead sale: first, to the discharge of all liens and encumbrances on the property; second, to the judgment debtor in the amount of the applicable homestead exemption; third, to the levying officer for unreimbursed costs; fourth, to the judgment creditor, first for costs and interest accruing after the writ issued and then for the amount due on the judgment; and fifth, any amount remaining to the judgment debtor. Under this priority order, existing liens and encumbrances on the property are paid before the judgment debtor receives the exempt amount, and the judgment debtor receives the exempt amount before the judgment creditor is paid anything toward satisfying the judgment.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The levying officer shall distribute the proceeds of sale of a homestead in the following order:(1) To the discharge of all liens and encumbrances, if any, on the property. (2) To the judgment debtor in the amount of any applicable exemption of proceeds pursuant to Section 704.720.(3) To the levying officer for the reimbursement of the levying officer’s costs for which an advance has not been made.(4) To the judgment creditor to satisfy the following:(A) First, costs and interest accruing after issuance of the writ pursuant to which the sale is conducted.(B) Second, the amount due on the judgment with costs and interest, as entered on the writ.(5) To the judgment debtor in the amount remaining."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 704.850(a), California Code of Civil Procedure, order of distribution of homestead sale proceeds (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=704.850.)
  Known gap: This Information Sheet relies on a single statutory section, California Code of Civil Procedure § 704.850(a); no second, independent source is cited for this specific distribution order. Section 704.850(b) also makes Code of Civil Procedure §§ 701.820 and 701.830 applicable to distribution of these proceeds; this Information Sheet does not describe what those two additional, cross-referenced sections provide.
